interactive.title: A family of curves
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on a family of curves. Each graph shows a rule, y against x, with a tangent: a short straight line touching the curve at one point, whose slope a readout gives. The first screens put the power rule beside its reverse, as two arrows: forwards, x³ becomes 3x²; backwards, the two steps happen in turn, add one to the power, then divide by the new power, and then differentiating the answer brings back what you started with. Then the family itself: the curve y = x² + c with a slider for c. Adding c lifts every point of the curve by the same amount, so the whole curve slides up or down without changing its steepness anywhere. The tangent at x = 2 keeps a slope of 2 × 2 = 4, from the derivative 2x, while its height, 4 + c, changes. Faint copies show other members of the family, all the same shape. Then a capacitor's charge curves, q = 0.5t² + c coulombs for a current of t amps, with a known value marked as a point, 3 C at 0 s: the slider moves the curve until it passes through that point, at c = 3, and that curve then gives 11 C at 4 s. Then a boat's distance curves, s = t² + c metres for a speed of 2t metres per second, with its start, 10 m out from the quay at 0 s, marked. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is shown going wrong on the graph, its curve missing the marked point or its slope not matching.
interactive.ignores: Every rule is an example, chosen so the numbers come out exactly. A current that keeps rising steadily is not how a capacitor charges from a steady supply through a resistor; there the current is largest at the start and falls away as it fills. The boat moves in a straight line. Only a few members of the family are drawn, but c can be any number, fractions and minus numbers included. The rule here is for powers of x; other functions, such as the sine waves of a.c., have reverses of their own, not shown.

explain.text:
[[Integrating]] is differentiating run backwards: you are given a rate and asked for the rule it came from.[^3] You already know the forward direction. The power rule takes x³ to 3x², so the question "whose derivative is 3x²?" has the answer x³. To answer such questions without guessing, undo the power rule's two steps in the opposite order.[^4] Forwards, you bring the power to the front, then take one off the power. Backwards, you add one to the power, then divide by the new power,[^4] so xⁿ becomes xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1). For x², add one to get x³, then divide by 3 to get x³ ÷ 3. Check it by differentiating: the power rule gives 3x² ÷ 3 = x², what you started with. The same happens for any power: differentiating xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1) brings the n + 1 to the front and takes one off the power, giving (n + 1)xⁿ ÷ (n + 1) = xⁿ, so the two steps cancel. A number in front carries through and a sum is done term by term, because differentiating works that way forwards,[^5][^6] so 6x² + 4x + 5 becomes 6 × x³ ÷ 3 + 4 × x² ÷ 2 + 5x = 2x³ + 2x² + 5x. The plain 5 comes from 5x, whose slope is 5 everywhere. One power will not go: −1, which is 1 ÷ x, because adding one gives a power of 0 and you cannot divide by 0.[^1] A power below zero means ‘one over’; lesson 9 comes back to that.

Differentiating loses something, and you have to put it back. A plain number does not change as x changes, so its derivative is zero, and x² + 5, x² and x² − 3 all differentiate to the same 2x. On the picture, adding a number lifts every point of the curve by the same amount. Take any chord, as in lesson 1: both its ends are lifted by c, so its rise is unchanged, and so is its slope. That holds for chords however short, so the tangents keep their slopes too, and the curve slides up or down without its steepness changing anywhere: move the slider for c and the tangent at x = 2 keeps its slope of 4 while its height changes. So working back from 2x cannot tell you which of those curves you came from, and the full answer is the whole family, x² + c, where c stands for any number.[^7] That c is the [[constant of integration]]. The answer is written ∫ 2x dx = x² + c, the [[integral]] of 2x: the ∫ sign says integrate, and dx says x is the letter that changes. The constant is easy to get wrong: on one 2023 Advanced Higher question, Scottish examiners reported that many candidates made basic errors in applying a formula approach or in dealing with the constant of integration.[^2]

To pick one curve out of the family, you need one value you know: where the thing started, or where it was at some moment.[^8][^9] Remember the charge rule q = 0.5t² from Rates on the job, whose current was t amps? Run it backwards. Say a capacitor charges with a current that rises steadily, i = t amps after t seconds. Current is the rate charge flows, i = dq/dt, so the charge is the integral of the current: q = ∫ t dt = t² ÷ 2 + c = 0.5t² + c coulombs. Say it already held 3 C at 0 s. Put t = 0 in: 0.5 × 0 + c = 3, so c = 3 and q = 0.5t² + 3. At 4 s it holds 0.5 × 16 + 3 = 8 + 3 = 11 C. Leave the c out and q = 0.5t² says the capacitor held 0 C at the start, not the 3 C it did, and 8 C at 4 s, short by the same 3 C all the way along. Check both halves: differentiating 0.5t² + 3 gives t, the current, and at 0 s it gives 3 C, the start. The value you know need not be at the start: told instead that it held 5 C at 2 s, you would get 0.5 × 4 + c = 5, so c = 3 again, the same curve. **Integrating undoes differentiating:[^3] add one to the power, then divide by the new power, for any power but −1;[^4][^1] add + c, because a constant differentiates to zero;[^7] and fix c from a value you are given.[^8]**

analogy.text: Setting out a cable tray beside a ramp, the drawing gives you its fall, so much per metre. That tells you how much lower each point is than the one before, but not where the tray sits: the same fall fits a tray fixed at any height, each one the last slid up or down. One height you know, where it leaves the switch room, picks out the one tray. The fall is the derivative, the heights along the tray are the rule, and the known height fixes c.
analogy.breaks: A tray's fall is the same all along, so its heights make a straight line and fall times distance gives them. On a curve the slope changes from point to point, which is why you need the reverse power rule instead.

practice.text:
- Work term by term. For each power of the letter, add one to the power, then divide by the new power, keeping any number in front. A plain number k becomes k times the letter.
- Add + c once, at the end.
- Put in the value you are given, the start or the value at some moment, and solve for c.
- Write the rule out again with c as a number.
- Check twice: differentiate your answer and you should get the rate back; put in the given moment and you should get the given value.

**Rules of thumb:** integrating raises each power by one, differentiating lowers it by one. With no value given, c stays as c.

**Worked example:** Say a hoist's rope runs at a speed v = 3t² + 2 metres per second after t seconds, and the hook is 4 m along at 1 s. Integrate term by term: s = 3 × t³ ÷ 3 + 2t + c = t³ + 2t + c. Put in t = 1: 1 + 2 + c = 4, so c = 1 and s = t³ + 2t + 1. At 2 s the hook is 8 + 4 + 1 = 13 m along. Check: ds/dt = 3t² + 2, the speed, and at 1 s, s = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 m.

**Common mistakes**
- Leaving out the + c, or never finding it when a value is given.
- Dividing by the old power: x³ to x⁴ ÷ 3, which differentiates to 4x³ ÷ 3, not x³.
- Differentiating instead: lowering the power when you meant to raise it.
- Taking a known value as c when it is not at zero: 2 C at 1 s does not make c = 2.
- Using the rule on 1 ÷ x, the power −1 (a power below zero means ‘one over’; lesson 9 comes back to it), where it would divide by 0.

checks.label: Integration is the inverse of differentiation: every answer rule on these screens, differentiated by working out its slope from the rule at points right across, gives back the rate it was integrated from, with or without a number added

To find the antiderivative, do the opposite things in the opposite order: first add one to the power, then divide by the power; for every power from none up to the fourth the answer differentiates back to that power, and dividing by the old power instead does not
We cannot set n = −1 in the fraction 1/(n + 1): the reverse rule gives no answer for the power −1, where the new power is 0, and gives one for every other whole power from −3 to 4

The + c appears because when you differentiate a constant term, the answer is zero: at every setting of the slider for c, the tangent drawn on the family keeps the same slope while its height moves by c, every lift arrow is c long, and each member has the same slope as the one with no c at every point across

Determines the constant of integration from given conditions: on each screen with a known value, the c found from it puts the curve through that value, a value at a later moment of the capacitor gives the same c, and with that c the capacitor curve drawn passes through its known value

Determining and using a function from a given rate of change and initial conditions: each puzzle that gives a rate and a known value accepts only the curve found from both, and reads its answer off that curve
Every tangent drawn, on every screen and after every answer, has the slope its rule gives at its point and passes through that point on the curve

From the rules, by hand: x³ has slope 3 at 1; 2x² 4, a plain 2 0 and x² 2 at 1; x³ ÷ 3 has slope 4 at 2; x⁴ ÷ 4 1, x⁴ ÷ 3 4 ÷ 3 and 3x² 6 at 1; 6x² + 4x + 5 integrates to 2x³ + 2x² + 5x with slope 15 at 1; 4x³ − 6x + 2 is 0 at 1, and 12x² − 6 and 4x⁴ − 6x² + 2x have slopes 24 and 6 there; x² + c has slope 4 at 2 and height 9 at c = 5; the capacitor holds 11 C at 4 s with c = 3, 8 C without; the boat is 19 m out at 3 s, 9 m without c, 16 m from 2t; c = 5 for 6x² − 4x through 5 at 1, slope 10 for 6x³ − 4x² + 3; 3t² from 2 C at 1 s gives 9 C at 2 s, 10 C taking 2 as c, 8 C without; and the screens’ words quote these values
Every puzzle offers three different answers and accepts only the right one; each wrong answer is the slip it stands for

Before Check no puzzle gives its verdict: nothing red and the working ends in a question mark; a picked answer only draws its own rule; a right answer shows its fit with nothing red; every wrong answer shows its slip in red
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 5 s of its screen opening, and every pick’s or answer’s motion within 1.3 s

applied.problem: Two slips: term-by-term and number-in-front come from the sum and constant-multiple rules of differentiating (its sources), not the power rule; and the examiners quote is about one 2023 question and names formula errors or the constant, so "many candidates" overall overstates it.
